cards.explanation: The answer is fifty men to run ahead of him. Absalom, King David's son (2 Samuel 3:3), gets a chariot, horses and fifty men running out front. Fifty! I think those fellas had a lot of cardio ahead of them, and I get winded just stamping a batch.

The answer is True. Absalom calls out, "What city are you from?" (2 Samuel 15:2). It sounds like small talk, and I bet you could hear it from a mile away. Notice he asks it of folks heading to the king with a grievance.

The answer is False. Absalom says, "Look, your claims are good and right…" Nobody's getting told they're weak here, friends. I tell you, a man who hears "you're right" first will listen to whatever comes after.

The answer is that the king has no deputy to hear him. Absalom says, "…the king has no deputy to hear you." He tells the man his claims are good, then points at a gap in the king's setup. And look who just happens to be standing there at the gate.

The answer is judge. Absalom says, "If only someone would appoint me judge in the land…" Then he adds that everyone with a grievance or dispute could come to him, and he would give them justice. I notice, bakers, that he wishes for a judge's job right after saying the king has no deputy to hear the man.

The answer is that he takes hold of him and kisses him. When anyone approaches to bow down, Absalom reaches out his hand, takes hold of him and kisses him. Imagine going to bow and getting pulled in for a kiss instead. I think a man would walk away from that feeling pretty important.

The answer is hearts. The text says, "In this way he stole the hearts of the men of Israel." He didn't take anything with his hands except a hand to hold and a kiss. The stealing happened somewhere much deeper, friends.

The answer is Geshur of Aram. Absalom says he made the vow while living in Geshur of Aram. He says he promised that if the LORD brought him back to Jerusalem, he would worship the LORD in Hebron. That's what he tells the king, anyway.
The answer is True, friends. The king answers, "Go in peace…" Then Absalom gets up and goes to Hebron. That's what the king says to him.

The answer is "Absalom reigns in Hebron." The spies are told, "When you hear the sound of the horn, you are to say, ‘Absalom reigns in Hebron!’…" So a trip Absalom explained as a vow comes with instructions about a horn and an announcement across the tribes. I think that's a big gap between what he told David and what he sent out.

The answer is False. The two hundred men from Jerusalem were invited as guests. The text says they "…went along innocently, for they knew nothing about the matter." Poor fellas, I think they'd have packed differently if they knew.

The answer is sacrifices. While Absalom is offering the sacrifices, he sends for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's counselor, to come from his hometown of Giloh. The sacrifices are happening, and in the middle of them Absalom sends for the counselor. That's a lot going on at once, bakers.

The answer is that it keeps increasing. The text says, "So the conspiracy gained strength, and Absalom’s following kept increasing." Ahithophel, David's counselor, gets called in, and the crowd keeps growing. I think the king should be getting nervous about now.
